# Combining datasets: `join` and `merge` {#sec-m1-joins}

Almost no analysis uses a single table. The real work is combining: freight flows with
population, highways with municipal GDP, port facilities with IBGE codes. This
chapter is about making that combination and, above all, about **finding out what did not match**.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(readxl)

colunas <- c("ano", "perfil", "sh2",
             "pais_origem", "uf_origem", "cidade_origem", "instalacao_origem",
             "pais_destino", "uf_destino", "cidade_destino", "instalacao_destino",
             "tku")

cabotagem <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx", na = c("", "-"))
stopifnot(ncol(cabotagem) == length(colunas))
names(cabotagem) <- colunas

cabotagem <- cabotagem |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), str_squish)) |>
  dplyr::filter(tku > 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(uf_origem  = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_origem),
         uf_destino = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_destino),
         tku_bi     = tku / 1e9)

nrow(cabotagem)
```

## The types of join

We will use two small tables to see how each `join` behaves without noise: flows by
destination state (`fluxos`) and GDP by state (`pib`).

```{r}
fluxos <- data.frame(
  uf_destino = c("PR", "SP", "BA", "AM"),
  tku_bi     = c(4.8, 12.3, 3.1, 0.4)
)

pib <- data.frame(
  uf   = c("PR", "SP", "BA", "CE"),
  pib_bi = c(613, 2720, 400, 220)
)
```

### `left_join()`: keeps the left table

This is what you will use in 90% of cases: it keeps every row of the main dataset and brings in the
columns of the auxiliary one.

```{r}
fluxos |> dplyr::left_join(pib, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf"))
```

`AM` got `NA` because it does not exist in the GDP table. **That is information**, not an error. And
it must be investigated, never ignored.

### `inner_join()`: only what exists in both

```{r}
fluxos |> dplyr::inner_join(pib, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf"))
```

Careful: `inner_join` **silently drops rows**. Always compare `nrow()` before and
after.

### `full_join()`: the union

```{r}
fluxos |> dplyr::full_join(pib, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf"))
```

### `anti_join()` and `semi_join()`: the diagnostic tools

```{r}
# what is in the flows and has NO GDP
fluxos |> dplyr::anti_join(pib, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf"))

# what is in the GDP table and does not appear in the flows
pib |> dplyr::anti_join(fluxos, by = c("uf" = "uf_destino"))

# filters the flows, keeping only those with a match in GDP (without bringing columns)
fluxos |> dplyr::semi_join(pib, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf"))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## The routine that prevents errors when combining

Always, in this order:

1. `anti_join()` in both directions, to see what does not match.
2. `left_join()`.
3. Check `nrow()` before and after. If it grew, the key on the right is duplicated.
4. Count the `NA`s in the columns brought in.
:::

### Summary table

| Function | Rows kept | Typical use |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `left_join()` | all from the left | add attributes to the main dataset |
| `inner_join()` | only those that match | when the analysis needs both pieces of information |
| `full_join()` | all from both | consolidate complementary datasets |
| `anti_join()` | left without a match | **diagnosing** keys that do not match |
| `semi_join()` | left with a match | filter by a list of codes |

The base R equivalent is `merge()`, with the arguments `all.x`, `all.y`:

```{r}
merge(fluxos, pib, by.x = "uf_destino", by.y = "uf", all.x = TRUE)
```

## The row duplication problem

If the key of the right-hand table has repeated values, the `join` **multiplies** the rows.
It is the most common cause of inflated totals in reports.

```{r}
pib_dup <- dplyr::bind_rows(pib, data.frame(uf = "PR", pib_bi = 999))

nrow(fluxos)
fluxos |> dplyr::left_join(pib_dup, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf")) |> nrow()
```

Modern `dplyr` warns you about this if you declare the expected relationship:

```{r}
#| error: true
fluxos |>
  dplyr::left_join(pib_dup, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf"), relationship = "one-to-one")
```

Declaring `relationship = "one-to-one"` (or `"many-to-one"`) turns a silent error into
an explicit one. It is worth always using it in production routines.

## Fixing data before merging

In practice, the problem is never the `join`. It is the key. Four fixes solve almost everything.

### 1. Different type

```{r}
a <- data.frame(cod = c("4118204", "3548500"), valor = c(10, 20))
b <- data.frame(cod = c(4118204, 3548500), pop = c(156174, 418375))

class(a$cod); class(b$cod)
```

```{r}
#| error: true
dplyr::left_join(a, b, by = "cod")
```

```{r}
dplyr::left_join(a, dplyr::mutate(b, cod = as.character(cod)), by = "cod")
```

### 2. Lost leading zero

State, municipality and census tract codes read as numbers lose the leading zero.

```{r}
codigos <- c(1100015, 110001)
stringr::str_pad(codigos, width = 7, pad = "0")
```

### 3. Case, accents and spaces

```{r}
chave <- function(x) {
  x |>
    stringr::str_squish() |>
    stringr::str_to_lower() |>
    stringi::stri_trans_general("Latin-ASCII")
}

x <- data.frame(municipio = c("São Gonçalo do Amarante", "Paranaguá"))
y <- data.frame(municipio = c("SAO GONCALO DO AMARANTE", "PARANAGUA"), pop = c(104669, 156174))

dplyr::left_join(
  dplyr::mutate(x, k = chave(municipio)),
  dplyr::mutate(y, k = chave(municipio)) |> dplyr::select(-municipio),
  by = "k"
)
```

### 4. Composite key

A municipality name is only unique **within** its state. That is why the correct key is `municipality + state`.
Better still: the IBGE code.

```{r}
bonitos <- data.frame(
  municipio = c("Bonito", "Bonito", "Bonito"),
  uf        = c("MS", "PA", "PE")
)

area <- data.frame(
  municipio = c("Bonito", "Bonito", "Bonito"),
  uf        = c("MS", "PA", "PE"),
  area_km2  = c(4934, 1789, 395)
)

dplyr::left_join(bonitos, area, by = c("municipio", "uf"))
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Always use the IBGE code when it exists

The 7-digit code (`4118204` = Paranaguá/PR) is the official key and does not suffer from the problems
above. In module 2, `geobr::read_municipality()` brings this code together with the geometry, and in
module 3 `censobr` and `sidrar` use it as the identifier. Keep it in every intermediate table
you create.
:::

## Application: enriching the coastal shipping dataset

Let us add the **region** of origin and of destination to the flows, using an auxiliary table
of states. Before the `left_join`, the diagnosis.

```{r}
regioes <- data.frame(
  uf = c("AC","AL","AP","AM","BA","CE","DF","ES","GO","MA","MT","MS","MG","PA",
         "PB","PR","PE","PI","RJ","RN","RS","RO","RR","SC","SP","SE","TO"),
  regiao = c("Norte","Nordeste","Norte","Norte","Nordeste","Nordeste","Centro-Oeste",
             "Sudeste","Centro-Oeste","Nordeste","Centro-Oeste","Centro-Oeste","Sudeste",
             "Norte","Nordeste","Sul","Nordeste","Nordeste","Sudeste","Nordeste","Sul",
             "Norte","Norte","Sul","Sudeste","Nordeste","Norte")
)

# 1. what does not match, in both directions
cabotagem |>
  dplyr::anti_join(regioes, by = c("uf_origem" = "uf")) |>
  dplyr::count(uf_origem, wt = tku_bi, name = "tku_bi")

cabotagem |>
  dplyr::anti_join(regioes, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf")) |>
  nrow()
```

The diagnosis found what we already knew from @sec-m1-limpeza: the origin may be the
**ZEE/Continental Shelf** or **Indeterminado** (undetermined), which are not states. And they
account for a huge share of the TKU. An `inner_join` here would erase almost 40% of the data without
warning. The solution is to extend the auxiliary table to hold these categories explicitly:

```{r}
regioes <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  regioes,
  data.frame(uf = c("ZEE/PLAT. CONTINENTAL", "INDETERMINADO"),
         regiao = c("Offshore (ZEE)", "Indeterminado"))
)
```

```{r}
n_antes <- nrow(cabotagem)

cabotagem_reg <- cabotagem |>
  dplyr::left_join(regioes, by = c("uf_origem" = "uf"), relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  dplyr::rename(regiao_origem = regiao) |>
  dplyr::left_join(regioes, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf"), relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  dplyr::rename(regiao_destino = regiao)

# 3. the rows did not multiply
c(antes = n_antes, depois = nrow(cabotagem_reg))

# 4. no NA left in the columns brought in
c(origem = sum(is.na(cabotagem_reg$regiao_origem)),
  destino = sum(is.na(cabotagem_reg$regiao_destino)))
```

The join is validated. Now the matrix of flows between regions, in billions of t·km (the
regions are North, Northeast, Centre-West, Southeast and South):

```{r}
cabotagem_reg |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = c(regiao_origem, regiao_destino)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = regiao_destino, values_from = tku_bi, values_fill = 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1))) |>
  dplyr::arrange(regiao_origem) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Reading this table answers a planning question in a few lines: the largest
flows are **offshore to the Southeast** (about 70 billion t·km), followed by **North to
Northeast** and **offshore to the Northeast**. In other words: oil from the platforms to the
terminals in the Southeast and Northeast, and container cargo leaving Manaus.

### Stacking instead of joining

When the tables have the same structure (for example, one file per year), the operation is
`bind_rows()`, not `join`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
anos <- 2020:2025
arquivos <- sprintf("dados/cabotagem_%d.xlsx", anos)

serie <- lapply(arquivos, read_excel) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "i") |>
  dplyr::mutate(ano = anos[as.integer(i)]) |>
  dplyr::select(-i)
```

`bind_rows()` aligns the columns by name and fills with `NA` those missing in some
file. It is desirable behaviour, but it hides a column being renamed between years.
Check with `setdiff(names(a), names(b))` before stacking.
